source.title_on_document: The impact of AI-assisted composition tools on cultivating creativity among music students in Guangdong province

supplement.where: No supplementary material or appendix is referenced; the PDF ends with References on PDF p. 25 (printed p. 2814).
supplement.holds: Not stated. The main PDF itself contains the pre/post descriptive statistics (Table 5), post-test comparison statistics (Table 6), and composite-score distribution (Figure 6); no external statistical supplement is identified.

paper_design_summary: Music students from four institutions in Guangdong completed a stated 12-week course using a purpose-built generative AI composition platform or traditional composition instruction; the analyzed groups contain 60 students each (PDF pp. 5-7 and 15). The paper repeatedly calls the design quasi-experimental, but its flowchart explicitly says randomized assignment and the participant description refers to a randomization procedure, so it is coded as a reported field RCT with that inconsistency flagged (PDF pp. 5-7). Expert ratings compare student compositions on nine dimensions, with an additional entropy-weighted composite; the work is described as AI-assisted, but separate post-test AI-access restrictions are not stated (PDF pp. 9, 13-15, 18, 20-23).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Music students were assigned to the AI-assisted composition or traditional-instruction group. Figure 1 labels group division Randomized Assignment and gives n=60 per arm. The body text independently refers to a randomization procedure. The sequence, allocation implementation, and any institutional blocking or clustering are not described, and the abstract/methods also label the design quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: The randomization procedure was effective in creating comparable groups with similar distributions across gender, age, grade level, prior music experience, and primary instrument selection, ensuring valid comparison of intervention effects.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2794), section 3.1 and Figure 1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), section 3.1 continuation for real educational settings and conflicting quasi-experimental label; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 2796), section 3.3 paragraph below Table 1 for the quoted randomization claim.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration or registry is identified in the full PDF; research methods are on PDF pp. 5-8 (printed pp. 2794-2797).

arms.name: Experimental group: AI-assisted composition
arms.description: AI-assisted composition instruction using the AI-Assisted Composition Platform, including generating and revising musical material and integrating Guangdong traditions (PDF p. 5, Figure 1; PDF p. 6, section 3.2; PDF p. 9, Table 2). Assigned count from Figure 1; analyzed count from Tables 5 and 6 (PDF pp. 13 and 15).

arms.name: Control group: traditional instruction
arms.description: Traditional instruction and traditional composition approaches over the same stated intervention period; no AI tool is described for this arm (PDF p. 5, section 3.1 and Figure 1). Assigned count from Figure 1; analyzed count from Tables 5 and 6 (PDF pp. 13 and 15).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions, attrition, or missing-outcome handling are stated. Figure 1 assigns 60 students per arm, and Tables 5 and 6 analyze n=60 per arm. The separate 28-student instrument pilot explicitly did not belong to the primary study (PDF p. 6, printed p. 2795, section 3.2); it is not added to the main sample or treated as another intervention study. No intention-to-treat claim is made here.
participants.who: Music students from four institutions offering specialised music programmes in Guangdong Province; Table 1 lists sophomore, junior, and senior grade levels (PDF pp. 6-7, sections 3.3 and Table 1).
participants.quote: The primary source of information data was 120 music students from four institutions offering specialised music programmes in Guangdong Province.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2794), Figure 1 for assignment; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), section 3.3 for recruitment and section 3.2 for the separate pilot; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 2796), Table 1, Total Sample (n=120); PDF pp. 13 and 15 (printed pp. 2802 and 2804), Tables 5 and 6, n=60 per analyzed arm.

ai_tool.name_model: AI-Assisted Composition Platform (AICP); purpose-built platform integrating generative artificial neural networks; underlying model, version, and vendor not stated (PDF p. 6, printed p. 2795, section 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Interactive generative music-composition assistance: students generated and modified AI-suggested melodies, manipulated AI-generated harmonic progressions, used form/arrangement tools, and produced comprehensive compositions in a full-feature environment. Coded other because this is a music-generation platform, rather than an open text chatbot or a supplied fixed set of ideas (PDF p. 9, printed p. 2798, Table 2).

task.description: Music composition: develop original compositions combining melodic, harmonic, structural, and traditional Guangdong musical elements, culminating in final composition portfolios and expert assessment (PDF p. 9, Table 2; PDF pp. 11-12, Table 4).
task.duration: Stated 12-week intervention (PDF p. 5, printed p. 2794, section 3.1 and Figure 1). Figure 1 places intervention in weeks 1-12 and assessment in weeks 13-14, whereas Table 4 labels weeks 1-2 as preparation and weeks 13-14 as synthesis/evaluation (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 2800-2801). Time allowed per scored composition is not stated.

outcomes.name: Overall Creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Direct expert rating of overall creativity; listed first under the codebook preference, but the paper does not designate it as a primary outcome. Compositional Product Assessment Rubric (CPAR) applied to musical compositions; expert assessments are described in section 5.3 (PDF p. 17, printed p. 2806). Scores range from 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest), PDF p. 14 (printed p. 2803), Table 5 note. Table 7 states that compositions were scored by five expert evaluators (PDF p. 20, printed p. 2809). Tables 5 and 6 compare student compositional-ability scores with n=60 per group; coded participant for those group analyses. Aggregation across raters or portfolio pieces is not specified. Pre-test, post-test, and change scores are retained together as repeated measurements of this outcome, not separate outcomes. Question coded with_ai from the reported AI-assisted compositions (PDF p. 18, printed p. 2807, section 5.3), the AI-assisted group label in Table 7 (PDF p. 20, printed p. 2809), and the full-feature composition environment in the final Creative Synthesis module (PDF p. 9, printed p. 2798, Table 2). The paper does not explicitly specify AI-access restrictions during a separate post-test, so this coding does not establish unassisted retention; confirmation is requested in open_questions.
outcomes.delay: End-of-course post-test following the stated 12-week intervention; Figure 1 places assessment in weeks 13-14 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 2794), and Table 4 places final composition development and summative evaluation in weeks 13-14 (PDF p. 12, printed p. 2801). Coded immediate at the course endpoint; no elapsed delay in days or later retention assessment is stated.

Table 5 within-group change: Experimental M (SD) = 1.64 (0.76), Cohen's d = 2.16; Control M (SD) = 0.50 (0.49), Cohen's d = 1.02. The Table 5 effect sizes are within-group pre-post effects, distinct from the Table 6 between-group effect; no effect was calculated for this form.

outcomes.name: Entropy-weighted comprehensive compositional ability score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Composite calculated by applying data-dependent entropy weights to the nine expert-rated compositional dimensions (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 2810-2811, section 5.5 and Table 9). This is an aggregate of expert ratings, not an AI judge. The paper reports the ranked distribution of all 120 student compositions (PDF p. 22, printed p. 2811, Figure 6 and accompanying text). Rank-block distributions and excellence/competence thresholds are grouped here as summaries of this same composite. Weighting by variation in quality scores is not a measure of similarity or diversity of ideas across people. Figure annotations and prose disagree about the rank-block group counts; all quoted counts below are identified by source. Question coded with_ai from the reported AI-assisted compositions (PDF p. 18, printed p. 2807, section 5.3), the AI-assisted group label in Table 7 (PDF p. 20, printed p. 2809), and the full-feature composition environment in the final Creative Synthesis module (PDF p. 9, printed p. 2798, Table 2). The paper does not explicitly specify AI-access restrictions during a separate post-test, so this coding does not establish unassisted retention; confirmation is requested in open_questions.
outcomes.delay: End-of-course post-test following the stated 12-week intervention; Figure 1 places assessment in weeks 13-14 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 2794), and Table 4 places final composition development and summative evaluation in weeks 13-14 (PDF p. 12, printed p. 2801). Coded immediate at the course endpoint; no elapsed delay in days or later retention assessment is stated.

eligibility.reason: On the paper's explicit assignment account, all three criteria are met: Figure 1 says Randomized Assignment to AI-assisted versus traditional composition, corroborated by the randomization statement below Table 1 (PDF pp. 5 and 7); the sample comprises 120 music students, with 60 analyzed in each arm in Tables 5 and 6 (PDF pp. 6-7, 13, and 15); and expert assessments score musical compositions, including originality and overall creativity (PDF p. 6, section 3.2; PDF p. 17, section 5.3; PDF p. 20, Table 7 note). The platform is expressly generative (PDF p. 6, section 3.2). Field RCT coding follows the explicit randomization claims and real educational setting, despite conflicting quasi-experimental terminology (PDF pp. 5-6). AI-access restrictions at the post-test are not separately specified and are flagged for audit; no AI-removal condition or across-person content-diversity outcome is established.

one_line_finding: Among 120 analyzed music students, post-test overall creativity was 4.71 (SD 0.54) in the AI-assisted group versus 3.62 (SD 0.69) in the traditional group, with reported Cohen's d=1.77 and p<.001 (PDF p. 15, printed p. 2804, Table 6).
open_questions: Resolve the contradictory design terminology: the abstract and section 3.1 say quasi-experimental, but Figure 1 says Randomized Assignment and the paragraph below Table 1 describes a randomization procedure (PDF pp. 1, 5-7). How were students randomized, and was assignment individual or clustered by institution/class?

Confirm whether the Table 5/6 post-test scores are ratings of the AI-assisted final compositions or a separate test performed without the platform. The final module includes a full-feature composition environment and section 5.3 describes AI-assisted compositions, but explicit post-test access rules are absent (PDF p. 9, Table 2; PDF p. 12, Table 4; PDF p. 18, section 5.3). Current with_ai coding rests on the reported assisted compositions; an after_ai interpretation would require confirmation of AI removal.

Reconcile Figure 6 with its prose: figure rank-block Experimental/Control counts are 29/1, 15/15, 16/14, 0/30, while the text gives 27/3, 22/8, 9/21, 2/28 (PDF p. 22, printed p. 2811). Confirm the composite construction and threshold counts before extracting a pooled estimate.

Clarify the full scoring rubrics, rater aggregation, and participant-to-composition mapping. In particular, Creative Fluency is reported as a 1-5 expert rating rather than an idea count, and Expressive Range is not operationalized as a category count (PDF pp. 6, 13-15, and 20).

Section 3.2 lists a Creativity Assessment Battery with musical divergent thinking, compositional flexibility, and creative originality subtests, but gives neither sufficient scoring procedures nor separately identifiable results for those subtests; section 3.4 mentions MANCOVA without reporting its intervention estimates (PDF pp. 6-7). Are these results available elsewhere? No supplement is identified.

Clarify the assessment schedule: Figure 1 places the intervention in weeks 1-12 and assessment in weeks 13-14, whereas Table 4 places preparation in weeks 1-2 and final composition/summative evaluation in weeks 13-14 (PDF pp. 5 and 11-12). No later retention interval is reported.
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. The complete markdown was read from start through References; no appendix follows. PDF page numbers in this form are 1-based and printed journal page numbers are supplied alongside key locators. Tables 5 and 6 were checked with PyMuPDF text and table extraction; Figure 6 annotations were also inspected by rendering in memory. No effect sizes or other statistics were computed. One main intervention study is coded; the instrument pilot has no separately reported intervention comparison. Nine rubric dimensions and the entropy-weighted composite are retained as ten output outcomes. The CAB subtests are not separately coded because their output-scoring procedures/results cannot be confirmed from the PDF. Satisfaction, motivation, technology acceptance, and qualitative interviews are outside output-based creativity outcomes; their associations with the already-coded composition scores do not add outcome entries (PDF pp. 18-21, section 5.4 and Table 8). Table 10 gives additional correlations for existing dimensions, not new outcomes (PDF p. 23). The composite is not coded diversity: dispersion of quality ratings used to create weights does not compare idea content across people. The design, post-test access, scoring, and Figure 6 discrepancies remain explicit audit issues. No data or code URL is provided.
